description: Earth's Interior and Structure - Comprehensive question bank derived from Earths_Interior_and_Structure.pdf. Covers all bullet points, definitions, depths, compositions, seismic evidence, discontinuities, and exam traps.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the three main compositional layers of Earth?

options.D: Mantle, outer core and inner core

questions.explanation: The three main compositional layers of Earth are the crust, mantle and core.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: On what basis are the crust, mantle and core classified?
questions.explanation: The crust, mantle and core are classified mainly on the basis of chemical composition and material characteristics.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the approximate mean radius of Earth?
questions.explanation: Earth's mean radius is approximately 6,371 kilometres.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the approximate depth to the centre of Earth?
questions.explanation: The centre of Earth is approximately 6,371 kilometres below the surface, measured using the mean radius.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is a mechanical or physical layer classification of Earth?

options.B: Lithosphere, asthenosphere, mesosphere, outer core and inner core
options.D: Upper mantle and lower mantle only

questions.explanation: A commonly used mechanical classification includes the lithosphere, asthenosphere, mesosphere, outer core and inner core.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the approximate depth of the Mohorovičić discontinuity beneath continents?
questions.explanation: The Moho is commonly about 30-70 kilometres beneath continents, although its depth varies substantially by location.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the approximate depth of the Mohorovičić discontinuity beneath oceans?
questions.explanation: The Moho is commonly about 5-10 kilometres beneath oceanic crust.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the approximate thickness of Earth's mantle?
questions.explanation: The mantle extends from the base of the crust to the core-mantle boundary at a depth of about 2,900 kilometres; its thickness is approximately 2,900 kilometres.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the approximate thickness of Earth's core?
questions.explanation: The core extends from a depth of about 2,900 kilometres to Earth's centre at about 6,371 kilometres, giving it a total radial thickness of approximately 3,480 kilometres.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the approximate thickness of Earth's crust beneath oceans?
questions.explanation: The crust ranges from about 5-10 kilometres beneath much of the ocean floor.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the approximate thickness of Earth's crust beneath continents?
questions.explanation: The crust is commonly about 30-70 kilometres beneath continents.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a method used to study Earth's interior?
questions.explanation: Direct drilling to the core is impractical; the deepest boreholes reach only a tiny fraction of Earth's radius. Indirect evidence from seismic waves, gravity, magnetic measurements, meteorites and laboratory experiments is used.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why is most of Earth's interior not directly accessible to humans?

options.B: Extreme temperature, pressure and depth make direct exploration impractical
options.D: No technology exists to drill even 1 km

questions.explanation: The extreme temperature, pressure and depth make direct exploration of the mantle and core impractical.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is Earth's crust?

options.B: Earth's thin, outermost solid compositional layer consisting mainly of silicate rocks
options.C: The liquid metallic layer surrounding the inner core
options.D: The central densest layer of Earth

questions.explanation: The crust is Earth's thin, outermost solid compositional layer, consisting mainly of silicate rocks and forming the continents and ocean floors.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the main composition of Earth's crust?

options.B: Silicate minerals containing oxygen and silicon

questions.explanation: Earth's crust is composed mainly of silicate minerals containing oxygen and silicon, together with elements such as aluminium, iron, calcium, sodium, potassium and magnesium.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Is Earth's crust uniform in thickness?

options.A: Yes, it is exactly 35 km everywhere
options.B: No, continental crust is generally much thicker than oceanic crust
options.D: No, oceanic crust is always thicker

questions.explanation: No. Continental crust is generally much thicker than oceanic crust, and thickness also varies within continental and oceanic regions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the two main types of Earth's crust?
questions.explanation: The two main types are continental crust and oceanic crust.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Is the crust the same as the lithosphere?

options.B: No, the crust is a compositional layer while the lithosphere includes the crust and rigid uppermost mantle
options.D: No, the lithosphere is only the upper mantle

questions.explanation: No. The crust is a compositional layer, while the lithosphere includes the crust and the rigid uppermost mantle.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is continental crust?

options.A: The relatively thin, dense crust under ocean basins
options.B: The relatively thick, generally less dense crust that forms continents and continental shelves
options.C: The liquid layer beneath the mantle

questions.explanation: Continental crust is the relatively thick, generally less dense crust that forms the continents and the continental shelves.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the usual thickness of continental crust?
questions.explanation: Continental crust is commonly about 30-70 kilometres thick, although it may be thinner in some regions and thicker beneath major mountain belts.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the average density of continental crust?
questions.explanation: The average density of continental crust is approximately 2.7 grams per cubic centimetre.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why is continental crust generally less dense than oceanic crust?

options.A: It contains more iron and magnesium
options.B: It contains a larger proportion of relatively silica-rich rocks such as granite

questions.explanation: Continental crust contains a larger proportion of relatively silica-rich rocks, such as granite, which are less dense than the basaltic and gabbroic rocks that dominate oceanic crust.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which rocks are commonly found in the upper part of continental crust?
questions.explanation: Continental crust's upper parts include abundant granite and related rocks.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is oceanic crust?

options.A: The thick, less dense crust forming continents
options.B: The relatively thin, dense crust that underlies ocean basins

questions.explanation: Oceanic crust is the relatively thin, dense crust that underlies ocean basins.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the usual thickness of oceanic crust?
questions.explanation: Oceanic crust is generally about 5-10 kilometres thick, commonly around 7 kilometres.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the average density of oceanic crust?
questions.explanation: Oceanic crust has an average density of approximately 3.0 grams per cubic centimetre.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the general composition of oceanic crust?

options.B: Mafic igneous rocks, especially basalt at the surface and gabbro at depth

questions.explanation: Oceanic crust is composed mainly of mafic igneous rocks, especially basalt at the surface and gabbro at depth.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why is oceanic crust generally denser than continental crust?

options.B: It contains more iron- and magnesium-rich mafic minerals

questions.explanation: Oceanic crust contains more iron- and magnesium-rich mafic minerals, which are denser than the silica-rich minerals common in much continental crust.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Where is new oceanic crust mainly formed?

options.B: At divergent plate boundaries, especially along mid-ocean ridges

questions.explanation: New oceanic crust is mainly formed at divergent plate boundaries, especially along mid-ocean ridges, where magma rises and solidifies.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Where is oceanic crust commonly destroyed or recycled?

options.B: At convergent plate boundaries where one tectonic plate subducts beneath another

questions.explanation: Oceanic crust is commonly recycled into the mantle at convergent plate boundaries where one tectonic plate subducts beneath another.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which type of crust is generally thicker?
questions.explanation: Continental crust is generally thicker than oceanic crust.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which type of crust is generally denser?
questions.explanation: Oceanic crust is generally denser than continental crust.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which type of crust is generally older?
questions.explanation: Continental crust contains much older surviving rocks; oceanic crust is generally geologically young because it is continually created and recycled.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which type of crust is mainly basaltic and gabbroic?
questions.explanation: Oceanic crust is mainly basaltic and gabbroic.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which type of crust commonly contains granitic rocks in its upper part?
questions.explanation: Continental crust commonly contains granitic rocks in its upper part.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Does oceanic crust lie only beneath the deep ocean?

options.B: No, it underlies ocean basins including areas beneath deep oceans and parts of continental margins
options.D: No, it lies only beneath continents

questions.explanation: Oceanic crust underlies ocean basins, including areas beneath deep oceans and parts of continental margins; continental shelves are generally underlain by continental crust.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is Earth's mantle?

options.B: The thick layer of hot, mostly solid silicate rock between the crust and the core
options.C: The liquid metallic layer surrounding the inner core

questions.explanation: The mantle is the thick layer of hot, mostly solid silicate rock between the crust and the core.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Where does the mantle begin and end?

options.A: Begins at the surface and ends at 2,900 km
options.B: Begins at the Mohorovičić discontinuity and extends to the core-mantle boundary at about 2,900 km depth
options.C: Begins at 660 km and ends at 5,150 km
options.D: Begins at 5,150 km and ends at 6,371 km

questions.explanation: The mantle begins at the Mohorovičić discontinuity beneath the crust and extends down to the core-mantle boundary at about 2,900 kilometres depth.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the main composition of Earth's mantle?

options.B: Magnesium- and iron-rich silicate minerals including olivine and pyroxene groups

questions.explanation: The mantle consists mainly of magnesium- and iron-rich silicate minerals, including minerals in the olivine and pyroxene groups and their high-pressure forms.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Is Earth's mantle completely molten?

options.A: Yes, it is a global ocean of magma
options.B: No, most of the mantle is solid but can deform and flow very slowly over geological timescales
options.D: No, it is entirely rigid and cannot flow

questions.explanation: No. Most of the mantle is solid, but it can deform and flow very slowly over geological timescales because of high temperature and pressure.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is mantle convection?

options.A: The complete melting of the mantle
options.B: The slow movement of mantle material driven by internal heat and density differences
options.C: The rapid flow of magma to the surface
options.D: The rotation of the inner core

questions.explanation: Mantle convection is the slow movement of mantle material driven by internal heat and density differences; it contributes to the movement of tectonic plates.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the upper mantle?

options.A: The region from the surface to 100 km depth
options.B: The mantle region extending from just below the crust to a depth of roughly 660 km
options.C: The region from 660 km to 2,900 km
options.D: The region from 2,900 km to 5,150 km

questions.explanation: The upper mantle is the mantle region extending from just below the crust to a depth of roughly 660 kilometres, although the exact boundaries depend on the classification used.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the lower mantle?

options.A: The region from the surface to 660 km
options.B: The region from approximately 660 km depth to the core-mantle boundary at about 2,900 km
options.C: The region from 2,900 km to 5,150 km
options.D: The region from 5,150 km to 6,371 km

questions.explanation: The lower mantle extends approximately from 660 kilometres depth to the core-mantle boundary at about 2,900 kilometres.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the significance of the mantle in plate tectonics?

options.A: It is completely rigid and prevents plate motion
options.B: Heat-driven mantle dynamics and the mechanical behaviour of the upper mantle help drive and accommodate plate motions
options.D: It is the source of all earthquakes

questions.explanation: Heat-driven mantle dynamics and the mechanical behaviour of the upper mantle help drive and accommodate plate motions, including processes associated with ridges, subduction and mantle upwelling.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the D" (D double-prime) layer?

options.A: A layer in the upper mantle at 660 km depth
options.B: A complex region at the lowermost mantle immediately above the core-mantle boundary with strong thermal and compositional variations
options.C: The boundary between outer and inner core
options.D: The top of the continental crust

questions.explanation: The D" (D double-prime) layer is a complex region at the lowermost mantle immediately above the core-mantle boundary, where strong thermal and compositional variations occur.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is Earth's core?

options.A: The thick layer of hot, mostly solid silicate rock between the crust and the core
options.B: Earth's central, densest major compositional layer, consisting predominantly of iron and nickel
options.C: The thin, outermost solid compositional layer
options.D: The rigid outer mechanical layer of Earth

questions.explanation: The core is Earth's central, densest major compositional layer, consisting predominantly of iron and nickel with smaller amounts of lighter elements.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: At what approximate depth does Earth's core begin?
questions.explanation: The core begins at the core-mantle boundary at a depth of approximately 2,900 kilometres.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the approximate radius of Earth's core?
questions.explanation: The core has a radius of approximately 3,480 kilometres.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why is the core denser than the mantle and crust?

options.A: It is composed mainly of silicate minerals
options.B: It is composed mainly of dense metallic material, especially iron and nickel, and is subjected to enormous pressure
options.D: It is located at the surface

questions.explanation: The core is composed mainly of dense metallic material, especially iron and nickel, and is subjected to enormous pressure.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the two parts of Earth's core?

options.B: Liquid outer core and solid inner core

questions.explanation: Earth's core is divided into a liquid outer core and a solid inner core.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the main significance of Earth's core?

options.B: It contributes to Earth's internal heat and magnetic field through the geodynamo
options.C: It is the source of all seismic waves
options.D: It is the rigid outer layer of Earth

questions.explanation: The core contributes to Earth's internal heat and magnetic field; movement of electrically conducting liquid metal in the outer core generates the geodynamo.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is Earth's outer core?

options.B: The liquid metallic layer surrounding the solid inner core and lying beneath the mantle

questions.explanation: The outer core is the liquid metallic layer surrounding the solid inner core and lying beneath the mantle.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: At what approximate depth does the outer core begin?
questions.explanation: The outer core begins at the core-mantle boundary at approximately 2,900 kilometres depth.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: At what approximate depth does the outer core end?
questions.explanation: The outer core extends to the inner-core boundary at approximately 5,150 kilometres depth.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the approximate thickness of the outer core?
questions.explanation: The outer core is approximately 2,260 kilometres thick.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the physical state of the outer core?
questions.explanation: The outer core is liquid.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the main composition of the outer core?

options.B: Predominantly liquid iron and nickel, with lighter elements such as sulphur, oxygen, silicon, carbon or hydrogen likely present

questions.explanation: The outer core consists predominantly of liquid iron and nickel, with lighter elements such as sulphur, oxygen, silicon, carbon or hydrogen likely present in varying proportions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why is the outer core liquid?

options.A: Because it is under low pressure
options.B: Because the temperature is high enough to keep its iron-rich material molten at the pressure prevailing there
options.D: Because it is composed of silicates

questions.explanation: The temperature in the outer core is high enough to keep its iron-rich material molten at the pressure prevailing there.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why do S-waves not pass through the outer core?

options.A: Because the outer core is too dense
options.B: Because S-waves require material with shear rigidity, and liquids do not support the propagation of ordinary body S-waves
options.C: Because the outer core is solid
options.D: Because the outer core has no temperature

questions.explanation: S-waves require material with shear rigidity to propagate, and liquids do not support the propagation of ordinary body S-waves.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How is Earth's magnetic field generated?

options.A: By the solid inner core rotating
options.B: By the geodynamo: movement of electrically conducting liquid iron-rich material in the outer core, organised by Earth's rotation and convection

questions.explanation: Earth's magnetic field is generated mainly by the geodynamo: the movement of electrically conducting liquid iron-rich material in the outer core, organised by Earth's rotation and convection.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is Earth's inner core?

options.A: The liquid metallic layer surrounding the solid inner core
options.B: The central, solid metallic region of Earth surrounded by the liquid outer core
options.D: The thick layer of hot, mostly solid silicate rock

questions.explanation: The inner core is the central, solid metallic region of Earth, surrounded by the liquid outer core.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: At what approximate depth does the inner core begin?
questions.explanation: The inner core begins at the inner-core boundary at approximately 5,150 kilometres depth.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the approximate radius of Earth's inner core?
questions.explanation: The inner core has a radius of approximately 1,220 kilometres.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the physical state of Earth's inner core?
questions.explanation: The inner core is solid, despite its extremely high temperature, because the immense pressure raises the melting point of its iron-rich material.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the main composition of the inner core?

options.B: Predominantly iron and nickel, with possible small amounts of lighter elements

questions.explanation: The inner core consists predominantly of iron and nickel, with possible small amounts of lighter elements.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why is the inner core solid while the outer core is liquid?

options.A: The inner core is made of different elements
options.B: Pressure is much greater in the inner core, raising the melting temperature so it remains solid at the prevailing temperature
options.C: The inner core is cooler than the outer core
options.D: The outer core contains no iron

questions.explanation: Pressure is much greater in the inner core, raising the melting temperature of the material so that it remains solid at the prevailing temperature.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which is denser, the inner core or the outer core?
questions.explanation: The inner core is generally denser than the outer core because of its higher pressure and solid state.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the approximate temperature of Earth's inner core?
questions.explanation: Estimates commonly place inner-core temperatures at roughly 5,000-6,000°C, although values depend on models and experimental constraints.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the lithosphere?

options.A: Earth's rigid outer mechanical layer, consisting of the crust and the rigid uppermost mantle
options.B: The weak, ductile region of the upper mantle

questions.explanation: The lithosphere is Earth's rigid outer mechanical layer, consisting of the crust and the rigid uppermost mantle.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the origin of the word 'lithosphere'?
questions.explanation: The word lithosphere comes from Greek roots meaning rock and sphere.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the approximate thickness of the lithosphere beneath young oceanic regions?
questions.explanation: Lithospheric thickness varies greatly: it is commonly around 50-100 kilometres beneath young oceanic regions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the approximate thickness of the lithosphere beneath old continental interiors?
questions.explanation: Lithospheric thickness may reach 150-250 kilometres or more beneath old continental interiors.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are tectonic plates?

options.A: Large, relatively rigid pieces of the lithosphere that move over the more deformable asthenosphere
options.B: Pieces of the liquid outer core
options.C: Molten magma chambers in the mantle

questions.explanation: Tectonic plates are large, relatively rigid pieces of the lithosphere that move over the more deformable asthenosphere and interact at plate boundaries.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Is the lithosphere identical to the crust?

options.B: No, the lithosphere includes the crust plus the rigid uppermost mantle
options.C: No, the lithosphere is only the upper mantle

questions.explanation: No. The lithosphere includes the crust plus the rigid uppermost mantle.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the asthenosphere?

options.A: A relatively weak, ductile region of the upper mantle beneath the lithosphere that can deform and flow slowly
options.B: The rigid outer mechanical layer of Earth

questions.explanation: The asthenosphere is a relatively weak, ductile region of the upper mantle beneath the lithosphere that can deform and flow slowly over geological timescales.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Where is the asthenosphere located?

options.B: Beneath the lithosphere, broadly within the upper mantle; its depth and thickness vary by tectonic setting

questions.explanation: The asthenosphere lies beneath the lithosphere, broadly within the upper mantle; its depth and thickness vary by tectonic setting.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Is the asthenosphere completely liquid?

options.A: Yes, it is a global ocean of liquid magma
options.B: No, it is predominantly solid rock that behaves ductilely over long timescales; small amounts of partial melt may occur in some regions

questions.explanation: No. It is predominantly solid rock that behaves ductilely over long timescales; small amounts of partial melt may occur in some regions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why is the asthenosphere important in plate tectonics?

options.A: Its weak, deformable character allows rigid lithospheric plates to move relative to the deeper mantle
options.C: It is the source of all seismic waves

questions.explanation: Its weak, deformable character allows rigid lithospheric plates to move relative to the deeper mantle.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the low-velocity zone?

options.A: A region in the upper mantle where seismic-wave speeds decrease, commonly associated with the asthenosphere

questions.explanation: The low-velocity zone is a region in the upper mantle where seismic-wave speeds decrease; it is commonly associated with the asthenosphere, although the two terms are not perfectly interchangeable.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the mesosphere in Earth's mechanical structure?

options.A: The strong lower mantle below the asthenosphere and above the outer core

questions.explanation: In the commonly used mechanical classification, the mesosphere is the strong lower mantle below the asthenosphere and above the outer core.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: At approximately what depth does the mesosphere begin in simplified textbook models?
questions.explanation: In simplified textbook models, the mesosphere begins near the base of the asthenosphere, often around 660 kilometres depth, and extends to the core-mantle boundary at about 2,900 kilometres.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Is the mesosphere the same as the atmospheric mesosphere?

options.B: No, the solid-Earth mesosphere is a term for the lower mantle, whereas the atmospheric mesosphere is a layer of Earth's atmosphere above the stratosphere
options.C: Yes, both refer to the lower mantle
options.D: No, the atmospheric mesosphere is the lower mantle

questions.explanation: No. The solid-Earth mesosphere is a term for the lower mantle, whereas the atmospheric mesosphere is a layer of Earth's atmosphere above the stratosphere.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Is the lower mantle liquid?

options.B: No, it is predominantly solid but can flow very slowly over geological timescales
options.C: Yes, it is liquid like the outer core
options.D: No, it is completely rigid and cannot flow

questions.explanation: No. The lower mantle is predominantly solid, but it can flow very slowly over geological timescales.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a seismic discontinuity?

options.A: A boundary inside Earth where seismic-wave velocities, directions or other properties change abruptly
options.C: A seismic wave that travels along the surface

questions.explanation: A seismic discontinuity is a boundary inside Earth where seismic-wave velocities, directions or other properties change abruptly because of changes in composition, mineral structure, density or physical state.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why are seismic discontinuities important?

options.A: They provide evidence about the boundaries between Earth's internal layers and help infer composition and physical state
options.C: They are the source of Earth's magnetic field

questions.explanation: They provide evidence about the boundaries between Earth's internal layers and help scientists infer the composition and physical state of the interior.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following are major named discontinuities commonly studied in school Geography?
questions.explanation: The commonly studied discontinuities are the Conrad, Mohorovičić (Moho), Gutenberg and Lehmann discontinuities.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the Conrad discontinuity?

options.B: A seismic-velocity boundary reported within the continental crust, traditionally separating an upper, more silica-rich layer from a lower, more mafic layer

questions.explanation: The Conrad discontinuity is a seismic-velocity boundary reported within the continental crust, traditionally separating an upper, more silica-rich crustal layer from a lower, more mafic layer; it is not globally continuous and is often absent or poorly defined.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Who is the Conrad discontinuity named after?
questions.explanation: It is named after the Austrian seismologist Victor Conrad.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: At what approximate depth is the Conrad discontinuity found where identifiable?
questions.explanation: Where identifiable, it is commonly reported at depths of roughly 15-20 kilometres beneath some continental regions, but its depth and presence vary and it is not a universal boundary.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the Mohorovičić discontinuity?

options.A: The boundary between Earth's crust and mantle, identified by a marked increase in seismic-wave velocities
options.B: The boundary between mantle and outer core
options.C: The boundary between outer and inner core
options.D: A boundary within the continental crust

questions.explanation: The Mohorovičić discontinuity, or Moho, is the boundary between Earth's crust and mantle, identified by a marked increase in seismic-wave velocities.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Who discovered the Mohorovičić discontinuity?
questions.explanation: Croatian seismologist Andrija Mohorovičić identified the discontinuity in 1909 by analysing earthquake waves.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: At what depth is the Moho generally found beneath ocean floors?
questions.explanation: The Moho is commonly about 5-10 kilometres below ocean floors.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: At what depth is the Moho generally found beneath continents?
questions.explanation: The Moho is commonly about 30-70 kilometres below continents, with substantial regional variation.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the Gutenberg discontinuity?

options.B: The core-mantle boundary at approximately 2,900 km depth, where the solid mantle meets the liquid outer core
options.D: A boundary within the continental crust

questions.explanation: The Gutenberg discontinuity is the core-mantle boundary at approximately 2,900 kilometres depth, where the solid mantle meets the liquid outer core.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Who is the Gutenberg discontinuity named after?
questions.explanation: It is named after the German-American seismologist Beno Gutenberg.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What seismic evidence identifies the Gutenberg discontinuity?

options.A: A sharp increase in P-wave velocity
options.B: The sharp decrease in P-wave velocity and the disappearance of direct S-waves beyond the boundary

questions.explanation: The sharp decrease in P-wave velocity and the disappearance of direct S-waves beyond the boundary provide major evidence for the transition from solid mantle to liquid outer core.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the Lehmann discontinuity commonly referring to in school-level Earth-interior topics?

options.C: The boundary between Earth's liquid outer core and solid inner core at about 5,150 km depth
options.D: A boundary within the continental crust

questions.explanation: The Lehmann discontinuity commonly refers to the boundary between Earth's liquid outer core and solid inner core, at a depth of about 5,150 kilometres.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Who discovered the inner-core boundary?
questions.explanation: Danish seismologist Inge Lehmann inferred the existence of Earth's solid inner core in 1936 using seismic-wave observations.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the seismic evidence for the Lehmann discontinuity?

options.A: Changes in the behaviour and travel paths of seismic P-waves, including waves reflected or refracted at the inner-core boundary
options.C: The increase in S-wave velocity in the outer core
options.D: The reflection of Love waves at the Moho

questions.explanation: Changes in the behaviour and travel paths of seismic P-waves, including waves reflected or refracted at the inner-core boundary, support the existence of a solid inner core.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Is the term Lehmann discontinuity used for only one boundary in all scientific literature?

options.A: Yes, it always refers to the inner-core boundary
options.B: No, some literature also uses Lehmann discontinuity for a separate seismic feature in the upper mantle; context must be checked
options.C: Yes, it always refers to the Moho
options.D: No, it refers to the core-mantle boundary

questions.explanation: No. In school-level Earth-interior topics it usually refers to the inner-core boundary, but some literature also uses Lehmann discontinuity for a separate seismic feature in the upper mantle; the context must be checked.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How does temperature generally change with depth inside Earth?

options.B: It generally increases with depth from the surface towards the core, although the rate is not uniform
options.D: It increases only in the crust

questions.explanation: Temperature generally increases with depth from the surface towards the core, although the rate of increase is not uniform throughout Earth.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the geothermal gradient?

options.A: The rate at which pressure increases with depth
options.B: The rate at which temperature increases with depth inside Earth

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the approximate average geothermal gradient in the shallow continental crust?

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Does the geothermal gradient remain constant all the way to the core?

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the approximate temperature near the centre of Earth?

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the main sources of Earth's internal heat?

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is primordial heat?

questions.explanation: Primordial heat is the internal heat retained from Earth's formation, including energy released during accretion, impacts, gravitational compression and differentiation.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is radiogenic heat?

options.B: Heat generated by the radioactive decay of isotopes within Earth, particularly in the crust and mantle
options.D: Heat generated by friction between plates

questions.explanation: Radiogenic heat is heat generated by the radioactive decay of isotopes within Earth, particularly in the crust and mantle.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How does Earth's internal heat influence geological activity?

options.A: It drives mantle convection and contributes to plate tectonics, volcanism, earthquakes, mountain building and the magnetic field
options.C: It has no effect on geology

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How does pressure change with depth inside Earth?

options.B: It increases with depth because the overlying rock and material exert greater weight on deeper layers
options.D: It increases only in the crust

questions.explanation: Pressure increases with depth because the overlying rock and material exert greater weight on deeper layers.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the approximate pressure at Earth's centre?

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why is pressure extremely high at Earth's centre?

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How does density generally change towards Earth's centre?

options.B: Average density generally increases towards Earth's centre because of changes in composition and compression
options.D: Density increases only in the crust

questions.explanation: Average density generally increases towards Earth's centre because of changes in composition and the compression of materials under increasing pressure.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is Earth's average bulk density?
questions.explanation: Earth's mean density is approximately 5.51 grams per cubic centimetre.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why is Earth's average density greater than the density of common surface rocks?

questions.explanation: Earth's average density is raised by the dense iron-rich core and by the compression of materials at high pressure in the deep interior.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which major layer has the highest density?
questions.explanation: The inner core is the densest major region of Earth.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the relationship between pressure and density inside Earth?

questions.explanation: Increasing pressure compresses materials and generally increases their density, although composition and mineral phase changes also affect density.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are seismic waves?

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why are seismic waves important for studying Earth's interior?

options.A: Their speeds, paths, reflections, refractions and absence in certain regions reveal boundaries, composition and physical state
options.C: They are visible to the naked eye
options.D: They only travel through the atmosphere

questions.explanation: Their speeds, paths, reflections, refractions and absence in certain regions reveal the boundaries, composition and physical state of Earth's internal layers.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the two broad categories of seismic waves?
questions.explanation: The two broad categories are body waves, which travel through Earth's interior, and surface waves, which travel along or near Earth's surface.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which waves are classified as body waves?
questions.explanation: Primary waves (P-waves) and Secondary waves (S-waves) are body waves.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which waves are classified as surface waves?
questions.explanation: Love waves and Rayleigh waves are the two main types of seismic surface waves; older or simplified school terminology may group them under L-waves.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the epicentre of an earthquake?

options.B: The point on Earth's surface directly above the earthquake's focus or hypocentre
options.C: The deepest point of the earthquake
options.D: The point where seismic waves are recorded

questions.explanation: The epicentre is the point on Earth's surface directly above the earthquake's focus or hypocentre.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the focus or hypocentre of an earthquake?

options.A: The point on Earth's surface directly above the earthquake
options.B: The point inside Earth where an earthquake rupture begins and seismic energy is first released
options.C: The point where seismic waves are recorded

questions.explanation: The focus or hypocentre is the point inside Earth where an earthquake rupture begins and seismic energy is first released.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How are seismic waves recorded?

options.B: By instruments called seismometers or seismographs, which measure ground motion

questions.explanation: Seismic waves are recorded by instruments called seismometers or seismographs, which measure ground motion.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are P-waves?

options.A: Shear body waves in which particles vibrate perpendicular to wave travel
options.B: Compressional body waves in which particles vibrate parallel to the direction of wave travel
options.C: Surface waves that produce rolling motion
options.D: Surface waves that produce side-to-side motion

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why are P-waves called Primary waves?

options.A: Because they are the most destructive
options.B: Because they generally travel fastest through Earth and are the first seismic body waves recorded at a distant seismograph
options.C: Because they travel only through the primary layer
options.D: Because they are the only waves that exist

questions.explanation: They are called Primary waves because they generally travel fastest through Earth and are the first seismic body waves recorded at a distant seismograph.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Can P-waves travel through solids, liquids and gases?

questions.explanation: Yes. P-waves can travel through solids, liquids and gases because each can transmit compressional disturbances.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What type of particle motion occurs in P-waves?

options.A: Particles move perpendicular to the direction of propagation
options.B: Particles move back and forth parallel to the direction of propagation, producing compressions and dilatations

questions.explanation: Particles move back and forth parallel to the direction in which the wave propagates, producing alternating compressions and dilatations.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Are P-waves the fastest seismic waves?

options.B: Yes, P-waves are generally the fastest seismic waves that travel through Earth's interior and arrive before S-waves
options.D: All waves travel at the same speed

questions.explanation: P-waves are generally the fastest seismic waves that travel through Earth's interior and arrive before S-waves at a given station.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How do P-waves behave when they enter the liquid outer core?

options.A: They speed up and travel straight
options.B: Their speed decreases sharply and their paths are strongly refracted

questions.explanation: Their speed decreases sharply and their paths are strongly refracted as they enter the liquid outer core.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Do P-waves pass through Earth's core?

options.A: No, they stop at the core-mantle boundary

questions.explanation: P-waves pass through the outer core and inner core, but their speed and paths change at the boundaries between layers.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are S-waves?

options.A: Compressional body waves in which particles vibrate parallel to wave travel
options.B: Shear body waves in which particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction of wave travel
options.C: Surface waves that produce rolling motion
options.D: Surface waves that produce side-to-side motion

questions.explanation: S-waves, or Secondary waves, are shear body waves in which particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction of wave travel.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why are S-waves called Secondary waves?

options.A: Because they are the most destructive
options.B: Because they generally travel more slowly than P-waves and are recorded after P-waves at a seismic station
options.C: Because they travel only through the secondary layer
options.D: Because they are the only waves that exist

questions.explanation: They are called Secondary waves because they generally travel more slowly than P-waves and are recorded after P-waves at a seismic station.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Can S-waves travel through liquids?

options.B: No, because liquids do not support the shear rigidity required for ordinary shear-wave propagation
options.D: Yes, but only through the outer core

questions.explanation: No. S-waves cannot propagate through liquids because liquids do not support the shear rigidity required for ordinary shear-wave propagation.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Can S-waves travel through solids?

options.B: Yes, through solids, which can resist shear deformation
options.C: No, they cannot travel through any material

questions.explanation: Yes. S-waves travel through solids, which can resist shear deformation.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What type of particle motion occurs in S-waves?

options.A: Particles move parallel to the direction of propagation
options.B: Particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction in which the wave propagates

questions.explanation: Particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction in which the wave propagates.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why do S-waves not pass through Earth's outer core?

options.B: Because the outer core is liquid and cannot support the shear stresses needed for S-wave propagation

options.D: Because the outer core has no temperature

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does the S-wave shadow zone reveal about Earth's interior?

options.B: That Earth's outer core is liquid
options.D: That the inner core is liquid

questions.explanation: The absence of direct S-waves beyond certain angular distances from an earthquake provides strong evidence that Earth's outer core is liquid.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Are S-waves generally more damaging than P-waves?

options.A: No, P-waves are always more damaging
options.B: S-waves often produce stronger side-to-side or up-and-down ground motion than P-waves and can cause significant damage, but surface waves are frequently the most destructive

questions.explanation: S-waves often produce stronger side-to-side or up-and-down ground motion than P-waves and can cause significant damage, but surface waves are frequently the most destructive.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are L-waves in traditional school-level Geography terminology?

options.D: Waves that travel only through the core

questions.explanation: L-waves are commonly described as long-period or surface seismic waves that travel along Earth's surface and usually produce strong ground motion.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the two principal types of seismic surface waves?
questions.explanation: The two principal types are Love waves and Rayleigh waves.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are Love waves?

options.A: Surface waves that produce rolling, elliptical particle motion
options.B: Surface waves that produce horizontal side-to-side ground motion, generally perpendicular to the direction of wave travel, with little vertical motion

questions.explanation: Love waves are surface waves that produce horizontal side-to-side ground motion, generally perpendicular to the direction of wave travel, with little vertical motion.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are Rayleigh waves?

options.A: Surface waves that produce horizontal side-to-side motion only

questions.question: Why are surface waves often highly destructive?

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which elements are major constituents of Earth's core?
questions.explanation: The core consists predominantly of iron and nickel with smaller amounts of lighter elements.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which minerals dominate the mantle?

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which rock type dominates the surface of oceanic crust?
questions.explanation: Oceanic crust is composed mainly of mafic igneous rocks, especially basalt at the surface and gabbro at depth.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which rock type dominates the upper part of continental crust?
questions.explanation: Continental crust's upper parts include abundant granite and related rocks.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the lighter elements likely present in the outer core?

options.A: Sulphur, oxygen, silicon, carbon or hydrogen

questions.explanation: The outer core consists predominantly of liquid iron and nickel, with lighter elements such as sulphur, oxygen, silicon, carbon or hydrogen likely present in varying proportions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which elements are mentioned as present in Earth's crust besides oxygen and silicon?

options.A: Aluminium, iron, calcium, sodium, potassium and magnesium

questions.explanation: Earth's crust is composed mainly of silicate minerals containing oxygen and silicon, together with elements such as aluminium, iron, calcium, sodium, potassium and magnesium.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the physical state of the mantle?

options.B: Mostly solid but able to deform and flow very slowly

questions.explanation: Most of the mantle is solid, but it can deform and flow very slowly over geological timescales because of high temperature and pressure.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the physical state of the outer core?
questions.explanation: The outer core is liquid.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the physical state of the inner core?
questions.explanation: The inner core is solid, despite its extremely high temperature, because the immense pressure raises the melting point of its iron-rich material.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the physical state of the asthenosphere?

options.B: Predominantly solid but ductile, with possible small amounts of partial melt

questions.explanation: The asthenosphere is predominantly solid rock that behaves ductilely over long timescales; small amounts of partial melt may occur in some regions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the physical state of the lithosphere?
questions.explanation: The lithosphere is Earth's rigid outer mechanical layer.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the physical state of the lower mantle (mesosphere)?

options.B: Predominantly solid but can flow very slowly

questions.explanation: The lower mantle is predominantly solid, but it can flow very slowly over geological timescales.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: At which plate boundary is new oceanic crust mainly formed?
questions.explanation: New oceanic crust is mainly formed at divergent plate boundaries, especially along mid-ocean ridges, where magma rises and solidifies.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: At which plate boundary is oceanic crust commonly recycled into the mantle?

options.B: Convergent boundary where one plate subducts beneath another

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What drives mantle convection?
questions.explanation: Mantle convection is the slow movement of mantle material driven by internal heat and density differences; it contributes to the movement of tectonic plates.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What allows rigid lithospheric plates to move relative to the deeper mantle?

options.B: The weak, deformable character of the asthenosphere

questions.explanation: The asthenosphere's weak, deformable character allows rigid lithospheric plates to move relative to the deeper mantle.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which isotopes are mentioned as sources of radiogenic heat?
questions.explanation: Heat is produced by radioactive decay of isotopes such as uranium, thorium and potassium.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does primordial heat include?

options.A: Energy released during accretion, impacts, gravitational compression and differentiation

questions.explanation: Primordial heat is the internal heat retained from Earth's formation, including energy released during accretion, impacts, gravitational compression and differentiation.

questions.subject: General Science

questions.explanation: Oceanic crust has an average density of approximately 3.0 g/cm³, while continental crust is approximately 2.7 g/cm³.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which major layer is the densest?
questions.explanation: The inner core is the densest major region of Earth.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why is Earth's average density (5.51 g/cm³) greater than surface rocks?

options.A: Because of the dense iron-rich core and compression at high pressure

questions.subject: General Science

questions.explanation: The average density of continental crust is approximately 2.7 grams per cubic centimetre.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the average density of oceanic crust?

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: At what depth does the mantle begin?

questions.explanation: The mantle begins at the Mohorovičić discontinuity beneath the crust.

questions.explanation: The outer core extends to the inner-core boundary at approximately 5,150 kilometres depth.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: At what depth does the inner core begin?

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the radius of the inner core?

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the radius of the core?

questions.question: What is the thickness of the mantle?
questions.explanation: The mantle is approximately 2,900 kilometres thick.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the thickness of the core?

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the approximate boundary between the upper and lower mantle?
questions.explanation: The upper mantle extends to a depth of roughly 660 kilometres; the lower mantle extends from approximately 660 kilometres to the core-mantle boundary.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the D" layer?

options.A: A layer at the top of the mantle
options.B: A complex region at the lowermost mantle immediately above the core-mantle boundary

questions.explanation: The D" (D double-prime) layer is a complex region at the lowermost mantle immediately above the core-mantle boundary, where strong thermal and compositional variations occur.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the upper mantle boundary typically taken as in simplified models?
questions.explanation: The upper mantle extends from just below the crust to a depth of roughly 660 kilometres, although the exact boundaries depend on the classification used.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the approximate thickness of the lithosphere beneath old continental interiors?
questions.explanation: Lithospheric thickness may reach 150-250 kilometres or more beneath old continental interiors.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the approximate thickness of the lithosphere beneath young oceanic regions?
questions.explanation: Lithospheric thickness is commonly around 50-100 kilometres beneath young oceanic regions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the low-velocity zone commonly associated with?
questions.explanation: The low-velocity zone is a region in the upper mantle where seismic-wave speeds decrease; it is commonly associated with the asthenosphere.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Where does the asthenosphere lie?

options.B: Beneath the lithosphere, broadly within the upper mantle

questions.explanation: The asthenosphere lies beneath the lithosphere, broadly within the upper mantle; its depth and thickness vary by tectonic setting.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the depth range of the mesosphere in simplified textbook models?

options.B: From about 660 km to the core-mantle boundary at about 2,900 km

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which discontinuity separates the crust and mantle?

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which discontinuity separates the mantle and outer core?

questions.question: Which discontinuity separates the outer core and inner core?
questions.explanation: The Lehmann discontinuity commonly refers to the boundary between Earth's liquid outer core and solid inner core.

questions.subject: General Science

questions.question: What does the Moho represent in terms of seismic velocity?

options.B: A marked increase in seismic-wave velocities

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which discontinuity is associated with the sharp decrease in P-wave velocity?

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which discontinuity is associated with changes in P-wave behaviour at the inner-core boundary?
questions.explanation: Changes in the behaviour and travel paths of seismic P-waves, including waves reflected or refracted at the inner-core boundary, support the existence of a solid inner core and the Lehmann discontinuity.

questions.subject: General Science

questions.subject: General Science

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the particle motion in Love waves?

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the particle motion in Rayleigh waves?

questions.explanation: Rayleigh waves produce rolling, elliptical particle motion, combining vertical and horizontal movement in a way similar to ocean waves.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which seismic waves are often the most destructive?
questions.explanation: Love and Rayleigh surface waves are often the most damaging because they can produce large-amplitude ground motion at the surface.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the order of arrival of seismic waves at a seismograph?

questions.subject: General Science

questions.subject: General Science
